subject: Preventing Pareto smoothed importance sampling (PSIS-LOO) from failing

messages.author: 8c6a877154df740e
messages.subject: Preventing Pareto smoothed importance sampling (PSIS-LOO) from failing
parts:
Dear Stan,

I recently started using PSIS-LOO.
I am currently using Aki Vehtari's MATLAB implementation of PSIS-LOO, but this question applies also to Stan, so I think it's on topic here.

In my application of PSIS-LOO to my problem, for the majority of models of interest I find that a large fraction of the k ≫ 0.7.
Note that chains convergence was good, both via visual inspection and with values of R ≈ 1.
However, some of the reported LOO log-likelihoods were quite obviously nonsensical (compared to other datasets) -- which was not surprising due to the very high k values.
As a double-check, I performed a time consuming 10-fold cross-validation, finding that indeed in the above case PSIS-LOO was giving a few awfully wrong results (on the upside, results were in very good agreement with 10-fold CV for the models in which all k ≪0.7).

Maybe I am just very unlucky in that my current and first problem in which I apply this method is "difficult" for PSIS-LOO, but I suspect that this case might be not so uncommon?
I understand that the standard solutions (as per the Vehtary, Gelman & Gabry paper) are to sample directly from the LOO posteriors, use k-fold CV or a more robust model.
However, these solutions are not really ideal as they are all time consuming or require additional fiddling (I appreciate that MCMC and model evaluation are all about fiddling, but the less the better).

Is there any general method that we can apply beforehand to try and prevent PSIS-LOO from failing?
I have a few tentative ideas, but I wonder if there is already an empirical solution that people have been adopting, and that could perhaps be implemented directly in Stan if a model is detected to be "difficult".

Thanks!
Luigi Acerbi


PS: I posted a similar question on Cross-Validated, please feel free to answer there if you think that it's more appropriate (I am not sure how many Stan users are on CV, if there is an overlap I apologize for the cross-post).

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: Preventing Pareto smoothed importance sampling (PSIS-LOO) from failing
parts:
Hi Luigi, 

Unfortunately convergence to the posterior doesn't guarantee that the PSIS-LOO approximation to LOO-CV (or any other approximation to it) will be good for your particular model and data. What type of model are you fitting and how long does it take to run? Also, how large is a "large fraction"? Depending on the answers to those questions it might not be infeasible to sample directly from the LOO posteriors just for the problematic data points.

Jonah

messages.subject: Re: Preventing Pareto smoothed importance sampling (PSIS-LOO) from failing
parts: Hi Luigi,

On Wednesday, March 2, 2016 at 9:13:21 PM UTC+2, Luigi Acerbi wrote:
In my application of PSIS-LOO to my problem, for the majority of models of interest I find that a large fraction of the k ≫ 0.7.
Note that chains convergence was good, both via visual inspection and with values of R ≈ 1.
However, some of the reported LOO log-likelihoods were quite obviously nonsensical (compared to other datasets) -- which was not surprising due to the very high k values.
As a double-check, I performed a time consuming 10-fold cross-validation, finding that indeed in the above case PSIS-LOO was giving a few awfully wrong results (on the upside, results were in very good agreement with 10-fold CV for the models in which all k ≪0.7).
Great to know that the diagnostic worked in your problem, too :)
Maybe I am just very unlucky in that my current and first problem in which I apply this method is "difficult" for PSIS-LOO, but I suspect that this case might be not so uncommon?

For complex models with many parameters or non-robust models and model mis-specification it should not so uncommon. Maybe this is case in your problem, too?
PSIS-LOO is meant to save time in easy problems and khat diagnostic tells when you have easy enough problem that you can avoid extra work.

I understand that the standard solutions (as per the Vehtary, Gelman & Gabry paper) are to sample directly from the LOO posteriors, use k-fold CV or a more robust model.
However, these solutions are not really ideal as they are all time consuming or require additional fiddling (I appreciate that MCMC and model evaluation are all about fiddling, but the less the better).
We think that often high khat values indicate a problem in the model. In that case changing the model to be more robust and to fit better to the data is definitely not fiddling.
Is there any general method that we can apply beforehand to try and prevent PSIS-LOO from failing?

You can't guarantee that your leave-one-out posteriors are close enough to the full posterior, but by using robust model in the first place will make it more likely that importance sampling works well.

I have a few tentative ideas, but I wonder if there is already an empirical solution that people have been adopting, and that could perhaps be implemented directly in Stan if a model is detected to be "difficult".
I am not aware of any generic solution which would not require additional computation.

PS: I posted a similar question on Cross-Validated, please feel free to answer there if you think that it's more appropriate (I am not sure how many Stan users are on CV, if there is an overlap I apologize for the cross-post).

If you get useful answers in Cross-Validated, please post a note here, too, as I guess that many Stan users don't actively use that service.

Aki

messages.author: 8c6a877154df740e
messages.subject: Re: Preventing Pareto smoothed importance sampling (PSIS-LOO) from failing
parts:
Hi Jonah, Aki,

thanks so much for your prompt replies!

@Jonah:
What type of model are you fitting and how long does it take to run?

I am fitting a large number of models to a cognitive task (~30 models per 40 subjects).
Sampling from the posterior of each subject/model takes a few hours because the posterior is nasty and I need to sample a lot (~4*10^5 samples per chain) to achieve good mixing. I could improve sampling efficiency with HMC or other techniques (and that's why I am looking into Stan), but that's another point.
On my institution cluster I can run 200-300 processes at a time, so a basic analysis requires a couple of days. A 10-fold CV, on the other hand, requires weeks.

The models involve the inference of a latent "observer's belief distribution", which is observed experimentally only indirectly through a very noisy process that yields only "yes/no" responses. Different models make different parametric assumptions about the shape of the observer's belief distribution (e.g., Gaussian, Student's t, mixture of Gaussians with different properties, etc.).

This is not my model -- I am actually running this to check whether there are potential issues with this model, such as lack of identifiability, model mis-specification and over-fitting, as I suspect there are.
So, in some sense, given my prior, it's not so surprising that PSIS-LOO fails.
Also, how large is a "large fraction"? Depending on the answers to those questions it might not be infeasible to sample directly from the LOO posteriors just for the problematic data points.

For many models up to 2-5% of the trials (~20-50 trials), and for a few bad models or datasets, I've seen up to 25% (~250 trials).

@Aki:
For complex models with many parameters or non-robust models and model mis-specification it should not so uncommon. Maybe this is case in your problem, too?
Actually, yes, it is very likely the case here! (see my reply above)
We think that often high khat values indicate a problem in the model. In that case changing the model to be more robust and to fit better to the data is definitely not fiddling.

True, but sometimes we happen to be fitting a bad model as a part of a model comparison (we may or may not know beforehand that a model is bad).
It's somewhat counter-intuitive that we need to spend a lot of more computational resources for a model that we end up knowing is bad... just to show that it is really bad.
(I appreciate that the whole "model comparison" philosophy may be demodé here, but it is still pretty common in my field.)

You can't guarantee that your leave-one-out posteriors are close enough to the full posterior, but by using robust model in the first place will make it more likely that importance sampling works well.
I am not aware of any generic solution which would not require additional computation.

The solutions I am thinking of require some additional computation, although not as much as recomputing the LOO posterior (or k-fold cross validation).
Maybe there is some reason for which they wouldn't work -- I will think a bit more about it.

Thanks!
Luigi
